fixes.explanation: Malta it is, baker. Acts 28:1 says that once they were safely ashore, they learned the island was called Malta. After a shipwreck, I bet a name on the map felt like a warm blanket.

Crete is part of this voyage, but it's not the island they reach here (Acts 27:7). Acts 28:1 says that once they were safely ashore, they learned the island was called Malta. Malta is the name to hold onto for this stop.

Cyprus comes up earlier in this voyage (Acts 27:4), but this isn't it. Acts 28:1 says that once they were safely ashore, they learned the island was called Malta. That's the name to remember for this stop.

Dry cloaks would've been lovely, friend, but the text doesn't mention them. Acts 28:2 says the islanders "…kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold." The fire and the welcome are what the verse gives us.
A viper, baker. Acts 28:3 says it was "…driven out by the heat…" and fastened itself to Paul's hand as he laid sticks on the fire. I would have hollered so loud the whole island heard me.

Close in spirit, but a scorpion isn't what the text says. Acts 28:3 says a viper, "…driven out by the heat…" fastened itself to Paul's hand as he laid sticks on the fire. I think Paul was just trying to help with that fire, and the viper showed up anyway.

Yes, a murderer. In Acts 28:4 the islanders say to one another, "Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live." They saw the creature hanging from his hand and came to a big conclusion. I think we've all been quick to judge a situation we only half saw.

Not quite, baker. Acts 28:5 says Paul shook the creature off into the fire and "…suffered no ill effects." Acts 28:6 adds that the islanders waited a long time and saw nothing unusual happen to him. No ill effects, start to finish.

False is right. Acts 28:5 says Paul shook the creature off into the fire and "…suffered no ill effects." He just shook it off, like a man brushing crumbs off his apron. Then the islanders waited a long time and saw nothing unusual happen to him (Acts 28:6).

That's the one. Acts 28:7 says Publius "…welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days." Publius was the chief official of the island, and his estate stood nearby. Three days of hospitality is a real welcome.

Guards aren't what this verse says, baker. Acts 28:7 says Publius, the chief official, "…welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days." Hospitably is the word. Hosting beats holding, every time.

That's not what the text says, friend. Acts 28:8 says Paul went in to see him, and "…after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man." No oil is mentioned, just Paul going in to see him and praying.
Yes! Acts 28:9 says that after this had happened, "…the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well." It didn't stop with the father of Publius. I bet that was a lot of people to see.

The text goes wider than that, baker. Acts 28:9 says "…the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well." That's the sick on the island, not one household. There's no "only" anywhere in that verse, and I'm glad.
The soldiers aren't mentioned in this verse. Acts 28:9 says "…the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well." That's the sick on the whole island, not one group.
